findings.title: Rebasing stETH held by the PoolManager gains and loses balance outside pool accounting
findings.difference: stETH balances are recalculated on each Lido oracle report, normally daily, with no transfer. The change is positive on staking rewards and can be negative after slashing or penalties. Lido's integration guide lists Uniswap among applications that are not designed for rebasing tokens and recommends wstETH.
findings.mechanism: Pool accounting never reads token balances. Balances are read only in sync and in _settle, and the only credit from a balance is the increase between a sync and the settle that follows in the same transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). A positive rebase raises balanceOf(PoolManager) with no sync and settle around it, so the increase belongs to no pool, no position and no claim. The only outflows are take and collectProtocolFees (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), and both debit an accounted amount, so the surplus cannot be paid out to LPs. Someone who can run sync, the rebase and settle inside one transaction would be credited the whole rebase on the PoolManager's balance. For stETH the rebase happens inside submitReportData, which only an oracle committee member or a SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE holder can call. A negative rebase lowers the balance below the sum of pool and claim accounting, and the last withdrawals of stETH revert in Currency.transfer. Transfer rounding is safe for the PoolManager: a take debits the full amount while stETH moves at most that amount, and settle credits what arrived.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds 80.4539 stETH at block 26470360. LPs in stETH pools earn no staking yield on it; the yield accumulates as an unclaimable surplus. After a negative rebase the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws stETH last. wstETH (2,295 held) is not affected because its balances do not rebase.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use stETH or another elastic supply token as a currency. The loss case needs a negative Lido report. Capturing the positive rebase needs an oracle committee member acting through a contract or an EIP-7702 delegated account. I derived the rounding argument from the share formula in the Lido guide and did not test it on chain. I did not compute how much of the 80.4539 stETH is surplus.
findings.mitigations: Use wstETH in pools. Interfaces can warn on pools whose currency is stETH or another rebasing token. A hook cannot fix this because the surplus is not reachable through any delta.

A balance increase that has no sync before it and no settle after it therefore reaches no delta and cannot be paid out. A caller who runs sync, then the rebase, then settle in one transaction is credited the whole increase on the PoolManager's balance (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and sync needs no unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:279). I checked the rounding argument from the share formula: a transfer moves floor(amount * totalShares / totalPooledEther) shares, so the sender's balance falls by at most the amount that take debited. verification.corrections: I raise the severity from low to medium. Low is for hazards with no direct loss path. Here the staking yield on stETH held by the PoolManager is stranded for good, the increase is visible on chain, and the loss is limited to stETH pools and claims, which is the medium definition. The effect is closer to a permanent freeze of the yield than to degrade. The principal shortfall case needs a negative report, which the Lido guide says had not happened when it was written. The same sync, trigger, settle sequence applies to any token whose balance at the PoolManager a third party can raise inside one transaction, which is recorded as a lead.

findings.title: A take to a recipient whose receive policy rejects the PoolManager succeeds and strands the funds in ReceivePolicyGuard
findings.difference: Since T6 any Tempo account can set a receive policy in the TIP-403 registry: a sender list, a token filter and a recovery authority. When a TIP-20 transfer fails the recipient's receive policy, the transfer does not revert. The token credits ReceivePolicyGuard at 0xB10C000000000000000000000000000000000000, records a receipt and returns true. Only the recovery authority captured in the receipt can claim the amount. With recovery authority address(0) the claimer is the originator, which is the from address of the transfer. An ERC-20 transfer on Ethereum either credits the recipient or reverts.
findings.mechanism: 1. A user or a router calls take(currency, to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The caller's delta is debited and the PoolManager calls transfer(to, amount) on the TIP-20 (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). 2. The recipient to has a receive policy that rejects the PoolManager as sender, or filters out the token. The TIP-20 precompile moves the amount from the PoolManager to ReceivePolicyGuard with the PoolManager as originator and returns true. 3. The return value is 32 bytes of 1, so the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 passes and take completes. The recipient's balance is unchanged. 4. If the recipient's recovery authority is its own address or a third party, that party can claim. If it is address(0), only the originator can claim. The originator is the PoolManager, which has no function that calls the guard, so the receipt can never be claimed. 5. PoolManager accounting stays consistent, because the delta was debited and the balance fell by the same amount. The loss is the withdrawing party's.
findings.impact: The amount of each affected take is lost for good when the recipient's recovery authority is address(0), and delayed until a claim otherwise. This hits LP withdrawals and swap outputs sent to accounts that restrict senders, for example custodial deposit accounts with a sender whitelist. Pool reserves and other users are not affected.
findings.preconditions: The recipient must have set a receive policy that rejects the PoolManager address or the token, and must have chosen address(0) as recovery authority for the loss to be permanent. The party that names the recipient in take must not check the policy first. An attacker cannot set a policy for someone else. receivePolicy(PoolManager) is unset on chain, and the PoolManager cannot set one, so payments into the PoolManager are not redirected.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces on Tempo should call validateReceivePolicy(token, PoolManager, recipient) before a take and refuse or warn when it would block. Account owners who use sender whitelists should add the PoolManager address or set themselves as recovery authority. The deployer can document that withdrawals originate from the PoolManager address.

verification.factCheck: The receive policies page states that a blocked inbound TIP-20 transfer still succeeds, that delivery goes to ReceivePolicyGuard at 0xB10C000000000000000000000000000000000000, and that with recovery authority address(0) only the transfer originator may claim. The TIP-20 specification says a receiver policy rejection must not revert the transfer. In the client source, transfer returns Ok(true) when validate_transfer reports a blocked inbound, validate_inbound_or_block moves the amount from the originator to the guard, and for transfer the originator is msg.sender. claim in the guard reverts with unauthorized_claimer unless msg.sender equals the recovery authority resolved from the receipt. I tested it on chain. I read the ReceivePolicyUpdated logs of the registry over the last 30,000,000 blocks and found 19 events. Two accounts, 0xec0eca588024e2d0091e74bd9034ff581111ea7f and 0x5bfa9123fa9dc6448d24ebbdb59e98f237de70c3, have sender policy 0, which rejects every sender. validateReceivePolicy(OUSD, PoolManager, account) returns 2 for both. An eth_simulateV1 of OUSD.transfer(account, 1) from the PoolManager address returns true and emits Transfer from the PoolManager to the guard and TransferBlocked from the guard. Afterwards the guard's balance is up by 1, the recipient's balance is unchanged and the PoolManager's balance is down by 1. The guard's functions are claim(address,bytes) with selector 0xbb1757cf, balanceOf(bytes) and burnBlockedReceipt(bytes). eth_call from the PoolManager address to the guard with transfer(address,uint256) and balanceOf(address) reverts with an unknown selector error.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller's delta and calls transfer(to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The success test accepts a 32 byte return value of 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), which is what the TIP-20 returns for a redirected transfer, so take completes. Nothing in take reads the recipient's balance. The debit and the balance drop are equal, so PoolManager accounting stays whole and the loss falls on the party that named the recipient. The PoolManager makes outbound calls with four kinds of selector only: transfer(address,uint256) at src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, balanceOf(address) at src/types/Currency.sol:94, unlockCallback(bytes) to its caller at src/PoolManager.sol:110, and hook selectors to addresses with flag bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-134). The guard address has no flag bits and none of these selectors is claim, so a receipt whose originator is the PoolManager cannot be claimed. The tests have no token that returns true without crediting the recipient.
verification.corrections: The mechanism holds as written. Two points on reach. First, both accounts that reject all senders today name themselves as recovery authority, so they could claim a redirected amount. Three accounts have chosen address(0) as recovery authority, and all three currently allow every sender and every token. I found no account that is in the permanent loss configuration today. Second, a router that takes to itself and then forwards becomes the originator, and a router has no claim function either. The Universal Router and PositionManager on Tempo were not read. The severity stays medium. No third party can trigger the loss, pool reserves are not in reach, and the amount is limited to takes sent to accounts that set such a policy.

findings.title: Polygon system token at 0x1010 mirrors the PoolManager native balance and cannot be paid out by take
findings.difference: Polygon has a genesis contract at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 that presents native POL as a token. Its balanceOf returns the native balance of the account. Its transfer is payable and returns false unless msg.value equals the amount. Ethereum has no ERC-20 face of ETH at the protocol level.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync(0x1010) stores balanceOf(PoolManager) as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). That value is the full native POL balance of the PoolManager, which already backs pools that use address(0). 2. settle with 0x1010 synced credits the caller with any rise in that native balance since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). msg.value is rejected at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the PoolManager has no receive function, so the balance can rise only through a forced transfer such as SELFDESTRUCT. 3. take(0x1010, to, amount) calls transfer on 0x1010 with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73). The token returns a 32 byte zero. The success test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 fails and the call reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. collectProtocolFees for this currency reverts the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 4. A positive delta in currency 0x1010 can therefore only be cleared, minted as an ERC-6909 claim, or swapped. The POL that paid for it stays in the PoolManager native balance and no account holds a native delta to take it. 5. Double credit was checked and is not possible. A native settle while 0x1010 is synced reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:356, and sync(address(0)) clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283), so one POL is never credited under both currencies.
findings.impact: POL that a contract pays into a pool or claim denominated in 0x1010 cannot leave the PoolManager as that currency and is not claimable as native POL either. Pools that hold POL under address(0) are not affected. The PoolManager held about 3.1 million native POL at the time of the query. Protocol fees accrued in currency 0x1010 would also be stuck.
findings.preconditions: Someone initializes a pool with 0x1010 as a currency, and a custom contract forces POL into the PoolManager between sync and settle. Standard periphery cannot do this because approve and transferFrom on 0x1010 revert. The actor loses its own funds. No path was found that takes funds from other users.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and pool indexers on Polygon should refuse 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 as a pool currency and direct users to address(0) or WPOL. Block explorers label 0x1010 as the POL token, so the warning should be explicit in deployment notes.

findings.title: A payout sent to a HyperCore bridge address is credited to the PoolManager's HyperCore account and cannot be recovered
findings.difference: HyperEVM has bridge addresses where a plain transfer moves funds to HyperCore and credits the sender of the transfer. HYPE sent as value to 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 is credited to msg.sender. A linked ERC-20 sent to its system address (0x20 followed by the token index, for example 0x200000000000000000000000000000000000010c for USDT0) is credited to the from address of the Transfer event. Ethereum has no address where a transfer re-homes funds on another ledger under the sender's name.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every payout from pools is sent by the PoolManager itself. take debits the caller's delta and then transfers to the recipient the caller chose (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). collectProtocolFees does the same for a recipient chosen by the fee controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 2. For the native asset the transfer is a value call with empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48). The code at 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 accepts exactly that shape and emits Received(msg.sender, msg.value), and msg.sender is the PoolManager. For an ERC-20 the PoolManager calls transfer on the token (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75) and the token logs the PoolManager as from. 3. HyperCore credits the PoolManager address in both cases. 4. The PoolManager can never act on HyperCore. It cannot sign, and its only outbound calls are unlockCallback to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:110), hook selectors to the hook address (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155), transfer and balanceOf to a currency address (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75 and 94) and empty calldata value calls (src/types/Currency.sol:48). CoreWriter accepts only selector 0x17938e13 and reverts on anything else. 5. The caller's delta is debited before the transfer, so the caller pays in full for what gets stranded. An attacker gains nothing from doing this on purpose.
findings.impact: The swapper, LP or fee recipient whose payout was directed to a bridge address loses it for good. Pool reserves stay whole. A router or front end that tries to deliver swap output to HyperCore by passing the bridge address as the take recipient would strand every such payout. At the time of the review the PoolManager's HyperCore spot balance list was empty.
findings.preconditions: A caller or an integration passes 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 or a token system address as the recipient of take or collectProtocolFees.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends should reject 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 and addresses with the 0x20 system prefix as take recipients. To move output to HyperCore, take to the user or to the router first and bridge from that address. The fee controller should apply the same rule to collectProtocolFees recipients.

findings.title: The OP Stack wrapped native predeploy on Celo calls itself Wrapped Ether and WETH but wraps CELO
findings.difference: On OP Stack chains that use ETH for gas, 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 is canonical WETH. On Celo the same address is a live wrapper of the native asset, which is CELO, and it still returns name 'Wrapped Ether' and symbol 'WETH' because the L2 L1Block predeploy reports the gas token as Ether. The bridged ETH token on Celo is a different contract at 0xD221812de1BD094f35587EE8E174B07B6167D9Af.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager accepts any address as a currency and reads no metadata (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). It learns balances only through balanceOf (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). Anyone can obtain the predeploy token one for one by depositing CELO. A pool, hook, router table or price source that treats this address as ETH backed WETH values a CELO backed token at the ETH price. Liquidity placed against it at that price is bought with tokens that cost one CELO each, and the paired asset leaves the PoolManager through ordinary swaps. Swappers who buy the token in such a pool receive a claim on CELO.
findings.impact: Funds of LPs and swappers in pools that list 0x4200...0006 as a currency, and integrations that map that address to WETH across OP Stack chains. Pools on the bridged WETH or on CELO are not affected. The PoolManager holds none of this token today, and its total supply is 0.143 CELO.
findings.preconditions: Someone must create or join a pool with the predeploy as a currency while pricing it as ETH, or an integration must hardcode the address as WETH. Any account can do the rest.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and token lists for Celo should hide or relabel 0x4200...0006 and point to 0xD221...D9Af for ETH. Deployment scripts and routers should take the wrapped native address from Celo specific configuration. Pool creators should check that remoteToken() on a WETH candidate returns the Ethereum WETH address.

findings.title: Source disagrees with two interface comments and two test conditions, and none of the four changes who can move funds
findings.difference: None. These are differences inside the repository, between src and its own comments and tests.
findings.mechanism: First, src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says collectProtocolFees reverts if the contract is unlocked. The code checks only the caller and whether the currency is the synced ERC-20 (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). _isUnlocked is declared at ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 and nothing calls it. The tests agree with the code: they expect ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced in both lock states (test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039). Second, src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 says only initialize and updateDynamicLPFee can be called without unlocking. sync has no onlyWhenUnlocked modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279) and test/Sync.t.sol:36-41 calls it while locked. Third, test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut when amountSpecified >= 0 at a 100 percent fee, while src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-316 reverts only for amountSpecified > 0 and line 320 returns a zero delta for amountSpecified == 0. Fourth, Pool.t.sol:143 treats a zeroForOne price limit below MIN_SQRT_PRICE as out of bounds, while Pool.sol:328 also rejects a limit equal to MIN_SQRT_PRICE. I traced each one for a fund effect. Fee collection inside an unlock changes protocolFeesAccrued and the balance by the same amount and touches no delta. A sync outside an unlock only sets two transient slots that the next sync overwrites. The zero amount swap changes no state. The stricter limit keeps slot0.tick from reaching MIN_TICK - 1.
findings.impact: No loss or freeze found. A reader who trusts the two interface comments gets the wrong picture of when sync and fee collection can run. The fuzz test at Pool.t.sol:129 would fail on an input with amountSpecified equal to zero and a 100 percent fee if the fuzzer produces one.
findings.preconditions: None for the mismatch itself. I could not run forge in this environment, so I do not know whether the current fuzz seed reaches the failing input.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can correct the two comments, decide whether collectProtocolFees should use _isUnlocked or drop it, and align the two test conditions with the source.

The setter setIsUnlocked in src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol:27-29 is also unused by any test, which is a further sign that a lock check on fee collection was planned or removed. findings.title: sync runs while the manager is locked and fee collection ignores the lock, and the mainnet fee controller lets anyone trigger collection
findings.difference: On mainnet the protocol fee controller is a V4FeeAdapter contract whose collect and triggerFeeUpdate functions have no access check. Any account can therefore make the PoolManager execute collectProtocolFees and setProtocolFee at a moment it chooses, including inside its own unlock callback. Mainnet also lets several users' operations share one transaction through ERC-4337 bundles and EIP-7702 batches.
findings.mechanism: sync has no onlyWhenUnlocked modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), so anyone can set the synced currency and reserves at any point of a transaction, and the value stays until a settle or another sync in that transaction. collectProtocolFees checks the caller and then reverts only if the currency is an ERC-20 equal to the synced currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). It never calls _isUnlocked, which is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 with no caller. ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 describes the guard as depending on the unlocked state; the code does not. I walked the fund-moving paths for a gain and found none. Collection of the synced ERC-20 is blocked regardless of lock state, so the balance cannot fall between a sync and its settle through this path. Native settlement uses msg.value and no balance (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). Collection is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued with checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55) and the adapter fixes the recipient. A sync left behind by an earlier operation in a bundle is overwritten by the next sync and cleared by the next ERC-20 settle (src/PoolManager.sol:361). What remains is that a stale sync makes a later native settle with value revert with NonzeroNativeValue if its caller did not sync first (src/PoolManager.sol:356), and makes collection of that currency revert for the rest of the transaction.
findings.impact: No loss or lasting freeze found. Within one transaction, a party that runs earlier can make a later native settle or a fee collection revert.
findings.preconditions: For the revert cases the two parties must share a transaction, for example an ERC-4337 bundle, and the later party must settle native currency without calling sync first. This is my own reading of the code and has not been checked by a second reviewer.
findings.mitigations: Integrators should call sync immediately before every settle, including native, as the comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 says. The deployer can decide whether sync should require the unlocked state and whether collectProtocolFees should check it, and can correct the A12 text either way.

verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), and the repository's tests call it while locked (test/Sync.t.sol:36-41, test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1023). collectProtocolFees checks the caller and then reverts when the currency is an ERC-20 equal to the synced currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). The comment at src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says the call reverts if the contract is unlocked. The code and the tests at test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1038 behave otherwise. I traced the fund paths myself. The synced check does not depend on the lock, so collection of a synced ERC-20 always reverts and the balance cannot fall between a sync and its settle through this call. Collection of another currency during an unlock lowers the balance by at most protocolFeesAccrued (checked subtraction at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55) and changes no delta. Fees accrue in _swap before the swapper pays (src/PoolManager.sol:238), and the swapper's negative delta must be cleared before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112) or the whole transaction reverts, collection included. Native settlement credits msg.value only (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). A collection with the PoolManager as recipient leaves an ERC-20 balance unchanged and reverts for native currency, because src has no receive or fallback function. A sync left by an earlier caller gives a later settler credit only for a real balance increase since that sync, and a native payment then reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356), which test/PoolManager.t.sol:987-988 covers. I found no path that raises a settle credit or pays out more than accrued fees. This agrees with the researcher and answers the researcher's first lead from a second reading.

The repository's own tests expect the present behaviour, so the disagreement is between the code and two texts: the comment at src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 and assumption A12. The synced check as written rejects collection in more situations than a check tied to the lock would, so the difference removes no protection.

findings.title: Operator transaction filtering on Robinhood Chain can fail any exit from the PoolManager, including force-included ones
findings.difference: Ethereum has no party that can make a chosen transaction fail. Robinhood Chain runs the ArbOS 61 compliance filtering feature. Its sequencer drops transactions that involve an address on a restricted list, and an operator account can write any transaction hash into the ArbFilteredTransactionsManager precompile at 0x74. The state transition then skips that transaction, raises the sender's nonce and consumes its gas, even when the transaction was force-included from Ethereum. On chain, filtering has been enabled since 2026-06-24 10:00 UTC and one externally owned account, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7 with nonce 6,237, is the registered filterer.
findings.mechanism: Every way to move funds out of the PoolManager is a call made inside unlock: modifyLiquidity with a negative delta, burn of ERC-6909 claims, and take. The contract has no exit that works without a successful child chain transaction. Step 1: the sequencer simulates each transaction and rejects it when it breaks a configured rule. The documented rule types cover a restricted sender or recipient, CALL, CREATE, CREATE2 or SELFDESTRUCT against a restricted address, and token transfers from or to one. Step 2: a user who then sends the transaction through the delayed inbox on Ethereum gets it included after the delay, but the filterer registers its hash first and RevertedTxHook skips the EVM call. The client code checks only whether the hash is in the list, so the list is whatever the filterer writes. Step 3: the user's liquidity and claims stay in the PoolManager with no other route out. The same rules mean that a take to a restricted recipient, or a hook or token that calls a restricted address on every operation, makes the transaction unacceptable to the sequencer. If the PoolManager, the PositionManager, or a widely used token or hook were put on the list, every transaction that calls it would be rejected. I could not confirm which rule set Robinhood has configured or whether any core contract is exempt, because the list is held off chain as salted hashes.
findings.impact: Funds are frozen for the affected sender or contract and cannot be taken by the filterer through this path. At the time of the query the PoolManager on this chain held 21,321 ETH, 16.98M USDG, 1,321 WETH and 3,134 ANT stock tokens. A listing of one LP freezes that LP's positions. A listing of a shared contract freezes every position that depends on it.
findings.preconditions: The filterer account, the compliance list provider or the chain owner must act. No unprivileged party can add a hash or an address. A third party can cause rejection of someone else's transaction only if that transaction already executes code or transfers chosen by the third party, for example a hook that pays out to addresses the third party controls.
findings.mitigations: Nothing in core can restore a forced exit. The deployer can ask the operator for a written commitment that the PoolManager and periphery addresses are never listed and can monitor FilteredTransactionAdded events on 0x74. Pool creators on this chain should avoid hooks that call or pay addresses supplied by third parties. LPs should treat force inclusion as unavailable when sizing positions.

findings.title: Robinhood Stock Tokens and USDG let the issuer block, pause, burn or upgrade the tokens held by the PoolManager
findings.difference: The assets this chain is built for are issuer-controlled in a more concentrated way than a typical Ethereum token. All Robinhood Stock Tokens are beacon proxies behind one contract, 0xe10b6f6b275de231345c20d14ab812db62151b00, which is both the upgrade beacon and the access registry with isBlocked, blockAccounts, pause and upgradeTo. The shared logic contract has adminBurn(address,uint256) and pause. USDG is an upgradeable Paxos token with isFrozen and decreaseSupplyFromAddress. The PoolManager already holds both.
findings.mechanism: Step 1, block or pause: if the registry blocks the PoolManager address or a token is paused, the token's transfer call fails. Currency.transfer treats a failed call as an error and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed, so every take and every collectProtocolFees in that token reverts. Settling needs a transfer into the PoolManager, which a pause or a block on the recipient would stop as well. One registry entry covers every stock token at once, and A6 applies because one address holds all pools. An LP can still remove liquidity, take the other currency of the pair and call mint to hold the frozen side as an ERC-6909 claim, because mint moves no tokens. The claim cannot be turned into tokens until the block is lifted. Step 2, burn: adminBurn against the PoolManager lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) with no matching delta. Pool reserves, claims and accrued fees then exceed the balance. Takes keep succeeding until the balance runs out, and the last LPs and claim holders bear the shortfall. Step 3, upgrade: upgradeTo on the beacon changes the code of every stock token in one transaction, which removes the A4 expectation that token code is fixed. I read function selectors and view results from chain. I did not read verified source, so the exact transfer check against the registry and the role holders are unconfirmed. Stock token splits and dividends do not create a balance change, because they move uiMultiplier and leave balanceOf fixed.
findings.impact: At the time of the query the PoolManager held 3,134.87 ANT stock tokens and 16,984,261 USDG. A block or pause freezes the stock token side of every pool that uses the affected tokens. A burn creates a loss equal to the burned amount, carried by whoever withdraws last. The other currency in each pair stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The issuer (Robinhood Assets (Jersey) Limited for stock tokens, Paxos for USDG) or a holder of the relevant role must act. isBlocked(PoolManager) and isFrozen(PoolManager) are false today and both tokens are unpaused. No unprivileged party can trigger any of these functions.

findings.title: One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
findings.difference: This is a property of assets on mainnet, and mainnet protocol rules are the reference. USDC, USDT and PYUSD each let one issuer role block a single address. USDC blocks transfers from and to a blacklisted address. USDT blocks transfers sent by a blacklisted address and lets the owner call destroyBlackFunds, which sets that address's balance to zero. PYUSD blocks transfers from and to a frozen address and lets the asset protection role call wipeFrozenAddress, which sets the balance to zero.
findings.mechanism: All pools, all ERC-6909 claims and all accrued protocol fees for a currency sit in one token balance at the PoolManager address. take calls currency.transfer and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86), so once the address is blocked nobody can withdraw that token from any pool. collectProtocolFees fails the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). For USDC and PYUSD a transfer into the PoolManager also fails, so settle can no longer be funded in that token (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). For USDT the blocked address can still receive, so users can keep paying USDT in while nothing can leave. If the issuer then zeroes the balance, the pools keep their accounting but the tokens behind it are gone, which is the undercollateralised state described in A2. LPs can still remove liquidity, take the other currency of the pair, and convert the blocked currency's delta into ERC-6909 claims with mint, which does no token transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The claims stay unredeemable while the block lasts.
findings.impact: At block 26470360 the existing PoolManager holds 79,953,224 USDT, 63,053,277 PYUSD and 30,404,253 USDC. One blocklist transaction per token freezes that token for every LP, every claim holder and the protocol fee balance at once. A wipe by Tether or Paxos turns the freeze into a loss of the full balance. The other currency of each affected pool stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The issuer role must act: the USDC blacklister (0x0a06be16275b95a7d2567fbdae118b36c7da78f9), the USDT owner (0xc6cde7c39eb2f0f0095f41570af89efc2c1ea828) or a PYUSD ASSET_PROTECTION_ROLE holder. The PoolManager is not blocked on any of the three today. I found no way for an unprivileged party to cause the block directly. I did not research what legal or policy triggers each issuer applies to contract addresses.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot remove this from a singleton. Interfaces and LPs can treat issuer-controlled tokens as carrying whole-protocol exposure instead of per-pool exposure. Monitoring isBlacklisted, isBlackListed and isFrozen for the PoolManager address gives early warning. Routers can fall back to ERC-6909 claims for settlement when token transfers to the PoolManager fail.

findings.title: Blacklist and freeze roles on pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them on Monad and MegaETH
findings.difference: The dollar tokens that carry most pooled value on these two networks are issuer-controlled contracts. On Monad the PoolManager holds 15.9 million native USDC, 1.64 million mUSD, 1.52 million AUSD, 61.7 thousand USDT0 and a small USD1 balance. On MegaETH it holds 14.1 thousand USDm, the chain's own stablecoin, and 675 USDT0. Each token answers an on-chain query that asks whether a given address is blacklisted, blocked or frozen. Six of the seven show a non-empty EIP-1967 implementation slot. USDC on Monad has an empty EIP-1967 slot, answers admin(), blacklister() and pauser(), and Circle's design document describes the contract as upgradeable. The same mechanism was reported for the OP Stack chains in this cycle (op-stack-eth unit). This entry adds the on-chain evidence for chain IDs 143 and 4326.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager keeps the reserves of every pool, all ERC-6909 claims and all protocol fees for one currency in a single token balance. It reads that balance with balanceOf at src/types/Currency.sol:90-96 and pays out with transfer at src/types/Currency.sol:55-87. 2. If the issuer blacklists, blocks or freezes the PoolManager address, the token reverts transfers from it. Currency.transfer then reverts with ERC20TransferFailed at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57) fail for that currency in every pool. Circle's design document states that a blacklisted address cannot transfer tokens. 3. If the token also refuses transfers to a restricted address, nobody can pay the token in, the balance difference at src/PoolManager.sol:358-360 stays zero and swaps that need the token as input cannot settle. Whether each of the seven tokens refuses incoming transfers was not confirmed from source. 4. If the issuer can also destroy or reassign a restricted balance, the PoolManager's balance falls without a take. Pool accounting still shows the old reserves, so the last liquidity providers and claim holders to leave find transfer failing for lack of balance. The USDT0 audit by ChainSecurity states that the owner of the token contract can blocklist and destroy funds. This was not confirmed for AUSD, mUSD, USD1 or USDm. 5. All seven tokens sit behind an upgrade path controlled by the issuer, so the transfer and balanceOf behaviour the PoolManager relies on (assumptions A2 and A4) can change after pools exist. 6. A pause of USDC, mUSD or USD1 has the same effect as step 2 for as long as it lasts.
findings.impact: All reserves, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees held in the affected token across every pool on that network. At the time of the queries that is 15.9 million USDC on Monad in the largest case and 14.1 thousand USDm on MegaETH. A block or pause is a freeze until the issuer reverses it. Destruction of the balance is a loss for the liquidity providers of those pools. Liquidity providers can still remove liquidity, take the counter-asset and keep the affected token as an ERC-6909 claim through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), because mint makes no token call.
findings.preconditions: The issuer, or whoever controls the blacklister, owner or proxy admin role of the token, must act against the PoolManager address or upgrade the token. The isBlacklisted, isBlocked, isAccountFrozen, isFrozen and frozen queries all return false for the PoolManager today. An unprivileged attacker cannot do this directly. An attacker can only try to provoke issuer action, for example by routing stolen funds through pools, and issuers normally act against the attacker's own addresses.
findings.mitigations: Show the issuer controls of each currency in interfaces. Monitor the blacklist and pause events and the proxy admin of USDC, USDT0, AUSD, mUSD, USD1 and USDm for the PoolManager address. Liquidity providers who cannot accept this risk should avoid pools that hold these tokens. The deployer cannot remove the risk in the PoolManager, because one address holds all balances by design.

findings.title: USDC and USDT0 issuers can block the PoolManager address, which stops every pool in that currency, and USDT0's owner can burn the blocked balance
findings.difference: Ethereum has the same class of issuer control for USDC, so this is a property of the assets pools hold on HyperEVM and is listed for completeness of the per network picture. On HyperEVM the two main stablecoins are native Circle USDC at 0xb88339CB7199b77E23DB6E890353E22632Ba630f and USDT0 at 0xB8CE59FC3717ada4C02eaDF9682A9e934F625ebb. USDC has a blacklister role (0x33aa4e959132e49552cb754fb6585bdcdf874beb) and a pauser, and a blacklisted address can neither send nor receive. USDT0 has an owner (0xb64a89ad247a2d691a728bb6822a85eedd7fc541) that maintains a blocklist and can call destroyBlockedFunds on a blocked address. Both tokens sit behind upgradeable proxies. USDC is also the asset HyperCore treats specially under AQAv2, which raises the share of pool liquidity likely to sit in it.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, all ERC-6909 claims and all protocol fees in one currency share one token balance at the PoolManager address. 2. Every payout runs take, which calls transfer on the token with the PoolManager as sender and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 3. If the USDC blacklister lists the PoolManager, or the USDC pauser pauses the token, every USDC transfer from or to the PoolManager reverts. take of USDC fails for all pools and inbound payment fails too, so the balance check in settle never sees new funds (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). 4. If the USDT0 owner blocks the PoolManager, transfers out revert while transfers in still succeed, so users can pay in and nobody can take out. The owner can then call destroyBlockedFunds and burn the whole PoolManager balance. Pool state still says the tokens are owed, and every later take of USDT0 fails for lack of balance. 5. modifyLiquidity and swap only move deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184 and 187-227). An LP can still remove liquidity, take the other currency and call mint to hold the blocked currency as an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The claim is redeemable only if the block is lifted.
findings.impact: All USDC or all USDT0 held by the PoolManager across every pool, plus claims and protocol fees in that currency. A block freezes them. destroyBlockedFunds on USDT0 removes them for good. The other currency of each affected pool stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The token issuer acts against the PoolManager address: Circle's blacklister or pauser for USDC, the USDT0 owner for USDT0, or the proxy admin of either token through an upgrade. No unprivileged party can trigger this. On-chain reads at block 51,941,800 show isBlacklisted(PoolManager) false, paused() false and isBlocked(PoolManager) false.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot remove the control. LPs can limit exposure by choosing pool pairs with that risk in mind. Front ends can watch for Blacklisted and BlockPlaced events that name the PoolManager and tell LPs to exit the other side of each pool with take and to hold the blocked side with mint. Integrators should not treat ERC-6909 claims in these currencies as equal to the token while a block is in force.

findings.title: Celo governance can move native CELO out of the PoolManager through the CELO token proxy and the transfer precompile
findings.difference: On Ethereum no contract can debit ETH from another account. On Celo a precompile at 0xfd transfers native CELO from any address named in its input to any other address. The precompile accepts calls only from the CELO token address 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438. That address is an upgradeable proxy owned by the Celo Governance contract.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager keeps native CELO as its own account balance. Pools that use currency address(0) and pools that use the CELO token address both draw on that balance (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96, and the on-chain balances are equal). The precompile reads the debited account from its first argument and checks only the caller. The current token implementation passes msg.sender or an allowance checked from address. A new implementation installed through _setImplementation could pass the PoolManager address as from and any recipient as to. The PoolManager has no code that runs on such a debit and no way to veto it. After the debit, take for either CELO currency pays out until the balance is exhausted (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), so the last LPs to withdraw bear the loss. A new implementation that makes transfer revert would freeze every pool that uses the CELO token address, because take calls transfer on it (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). Pools that use address(0) would still pay out by value transfer in that case. Governance returns stage durations of 1 day, 7 days and 3 days, which this review reads as approval, referendum and execution, so a standard proposal is public for days before it can execute. The hotfix path needs the approver multisig and the Security Council and has a 1 day execution window with no referendum.
findings.impact: All native CELO in the PoolManager, 6,167.7 CELO at the time of the query, across both currency faces. Every CELO holder on the chain carries the same exposure. Other tokens in the PoolManager are not reachable by this path.
findings.preconditions: A Celo governance proposal or a hotfix approved by the approver multisig and the Security Council must replace the CELO token implementation. No unprivileged path was found: an eth_call to the precompile from an address other than the token fails, and _setImplementation reverts for a sender other than Governance.
findings.mitigations: Watch the value of _getImplementation() on the CELO token proxy and the Governance contract for queued proposals and hotfixes that target 0x471E...a438. The referendum stage gives LPs days to withdraw before a standard proposal executes. A hotfix gives no such window. LPs who want protection from a token contract that reverts can use pools with currency address(0), which pay out without calling the token.

findings.title: B20 precompile tokens on Base give the issuer seize, pause and policy control over the PoolManager balance, and their rules change at hard forks
findings.difference: Since the Beryl upgrade on 25 June 2026, Base has a native token standard called B20. Anyone can create a token through a factory precompile at 0xB20f000000000000000000000000000000000000, and all B20 tokens share logic that runs natively in the node. Each token has role gated mint, burn and seizeWithMemo, a pause switch per feature, and policy slots that are checked on every transfer against the sender, the receiver and msg.sender. The policies are allowlists or blocklists stored in a shared Policy Registry precompile, and one policy can back many tokens and be administered by a third party. Base changes the shared logic at hard forks: Cobalt added seize, and Denim on 5 November 2026 started to enforce the executor policy on plain transfer calls. Ethereum has no enshrined token logic of this kind.
findings.mechanism: 1. A pool is created with a B20 token as one currency. Users pay in with sync, a token transfer and settle, which credits balanceOf(PoolManager) minus the synced reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). 2. Every payout calls transfer on the token with the PoolManager as msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). For a B20 token that call passes through the TRANSFER pause check, then TRANSFER_EXECUTOR_POLICY on msg.sender, TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY on from, and TRANSFER_RECEIVER_POLICY on to. msg.sender and from are both the PoolManager. 3. If the token admin pauses TRANSFER, binds a policy that does not authorise the PoolManager, or the admin of a referenced policy removes the PoolManager from an allowlist or adds it to a blocklist, the transfer reverts and take reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. Every pool, every ERC-6909 claim and the protocol fee balance in that currency are stuck together because they share one holder address. collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer path (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 4. If the issuer has configured SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY so that the PoolManager is not exempt, an account with SEIZE_ROLE can call seizeWithMemo(PoolManager, to, amount, memo). The seize skips allowances and the three transfer policies. The PoolManager balance falls without any delta being recorded, so the pools hold less than their accounting says, and the last LPs and claim holders to withdraw cannot be paid. 5. A hard fork can produce the freeze in step 3 with no action by the issuer after pool creation. Before Denim a token with a restrictive executor allowlist still allowed holder initiated transfer, so the PoolManager could pay out. Since Denim the same token rejects transfer from any msg.sender that is not on the executor allowlist. 6. A seize or pause in the middle of a settlement cannot be turned into credit: a lower balance makes reservesNow minus reservesBefore underflow and revert (src/PoolManager.sol:360).
findings.impact: All liquidity, ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees held in the affected B20 token on Base. A seize is a direct loss for LPs of that token. A pause or policy change freezes the token side of every pool that uses it. The other currency of each pool is not affected. Which B20 tokens the Base PoolManager holds today, and in what amounts, could not be listed in this cycle because the public RPC rate limited log queries and the Base explorer blocked the request. The PoolManager's ETH, WETH and USDC on Base are not B20 tokens: the factory returns false for isB20(USDC).
findings.preconditions: A B20 token with market value is used in v4 pools on Base. For a freeze, the token admin, the pauser, or the admin of a policy the token references must act, or a Base hard fork must tighten enforcement for a configuration the token already has. For a seize, the issuer must hold SEIZE_ROLE and must have set SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY to a policy that does not authorise the PoolManager. With the slot unset no account is seizable. An unprivileged attacker cannot do any of this to a token issued by someone else. An attacker who issues their own B20 token gets no more than a hostile ERC-20 already gives on any chain.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators and LPs should read, for every B20 currency, the three transfer policy slots, the seize policy slots, the holders of DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, SEIZE_ROLE and PAUSE_ROLE, and the admin of each referenced policy, and should treat a non renounced admin as able to freeze or seize. Front ends and routers on Base can call isAuthorized on the Policy Registry for the PoolManager under each bound policy and warn when it is false or when the policy admin is live. LPs caught by a freeze can still remove liquidity and keep the frozen side as ERC-6909 claims through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which does not call the token, and take the other currency. The deployer should track each Base upgrade changelog for B20 changes before activation.

verification.factCheck: All six Base docs pages were fetched and say what the finding reports. The upgrades page lists Beryl on 25 June 2026, Cobalt on 30 September 2026 and Denim on 5 November 2026 for Base Mainnet. The introduction states that B20 runs as precompiles in the node, that Base upgrades the logic through hard forks, that every token is created through the factory, and that TRANSFER, MINT, BURN and SEIZE can be paused separately. The policies page gives the scope table: sender policy on from, receiver policy on to, executor policy on msg.sender, and a policy admin who can change membership for every token that references the policy. The Cobalt note confirms that seizeWithMemo skips allowances and the three transfer policies and that an unset SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY makes no account seizable. The Denim note confirms that the executor policy now runs on transfer and calls the change breaking for tokens with a restrictive executor policy. On chain at Base block 60,794,561 on 22 November 2026: eth_getCode at the factory is empty, isB20(PoolManager) and isB20(USDC) return false, policyExists(2) returns true, and balanceOf and transfer on the uninitialised address 0xb200000000000000000001000000000000000001 revert. I also closed the gap the finding left open about exposure. The explorer lists recent transfers between the PoolManager and two B20 tokens. OUSD (name OpenUSD, 0xB2000000000000000000002fEb517dFeC7415344, isB20 true, code 0xef, 6 decimals): balanceOf(PoolManager) is 5,341,029 of a total supply of 93,186,135. Its TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY is policy 122, whose admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246 has no code. The other five scopes are unset, pausedFeatures is empty, and the PoolManager is authorised under policy 122 today. AMDC (name Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 0xB2000000000000000000000d8Ce462E99ee7A47B, 8 decimals): balanceOf(PoolManager) is 34.38. findings.title: Blacklist and freeze roles on the pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them, because one address holds all balances
findings.difference: The issuer model matches USDC on Ethereum, but the role holders are set per chain and several of the largest PoolManager balances in this unit are tokens that Ethereum pools do not hold in this form. On Soneium the bridged USDC.e returns one address, 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59, for owner, pauser and blacklister. On Ink and Unichain USD₮0 exposes isBlocked. On Ink USDG and on Soneium USDSC expose isFrozen. Circle USDC on OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain, World Chain and Ink each has its own blacklister and pauser address.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees for a currency sit in one token balance at the PoolManager address. 2. FiatToken transfer carries the modifiers whenNotPaused, notBlacklisted(msg.sender) and notBlacklisted(to). When the PoolManager pays out, it is msg.sender (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86, called from src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 3. If the blacklister lists the PoolManager address, or the pauser pauses the token, every take of that currency reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. sync still works because balanceOf is a view call. 4. The freeze covers every pool on the chain that uses the token, regardless of which pool or user caused the listing. 5. The freeze functions on USD₮0, USDG and USDSC were confirmed to exist by eth_call. Their effect on transfers and any balance destroying function were not read from source in this cycle.
findings.impact: At read time the PoolManager held about 12.25 million USDC on Base, 978,360 USDC and 180,746 USD₮0 on Unichain, 1.52 million USD₮0, 767,333 USDG and 676,274 USDC on Ink, 1.90 million USDSC and 517,001 USDC.e on Soneium, 323,556 USDC on OP Mainnet and 66,644 USDC on World Chain. findings.preconditions: The token's blacklister, freezer or pauser acts against the PoolManager address or pauses the token. This is a privileged issuer action. An unprivileged attacker cannot trigger it directly. A realistic trigger is a compliance response to tainted funds that were routed through a pool.
findings.mitigations: LPs can exit the non frozen currency normally and hold the frozen currency as ERC-6909 claims through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) until the listing is lifted. Integrators should monitor the blacklist and pause state of each large pooled token for the PoolManager address on each chain. For Soneium USDC.e, the deployer should identify who controls 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59 before treating it like Circle issued USDC.

findings.title: TIP-20 issuer roles can burn, freeze or pause the PoolManager balance of a Tempo stablecoin
findings.difference: On Tempo every stablecoin is a TIP-20 precompile with issuer roles built into the protocol. burnAt(from, amount), live on mainnet since T12 on 13 October 2026, lets a BURN_AT_ROLE holder burn any balance with no transfer policy check, unless the holder is on a protected list. burnBlocked lets a BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE holder burn the balance of an address that fails the sender policy. The protected list is FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve, ReceivePolicyGuard, the token's own address and Zone Portal addresses. The PoolManager is not on it. pause stops every transfer of the token. The admin of a TIP-403 policy can block an address for every token bound to that policy, and pathUSD and OUSD are both bound to policy 2, a blacklist administered by 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. Ethereum has no protocol-level burn of another account's ERC-20 balance. Each token there has whatever controls its own contract code contains.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees for a token sit in one TIP-20 balance at the PoolManager address. 2. A BURN_AT_ROLE holder calls burnAt(PoolManager, x). The TIP-20 precompile debits the PoolManager and reduces total supply. No PoolManager function runs. 3. The PoolManager tracks no per-currency reserve in storage. sync reads balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) and take pays out with transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75), so the claims recorded in pool state and ERC-6909 balances now exceed the tokens held. Withdrawals succeed until the balance runs out, then transfer reverts with InsufficientBalance and the remaining LPs and claim holders cannot exit. 4. The freeze variant: the policy admin adds the PoolManager to blacklist policy 2, or a PAUSE_ROLE holder pauses the token. Every take and every inbound payment for that token then reverts with PolicyForbids or ContractPaused, and settle cannot complete because the payment transfer fails. Once the PoolManager fails the sender policy, a BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE holder can also burn its balance. 5. If a burn lands between sync and settle inside one transaction, the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 reverts that transaction and nothing else changes.
findings.impact: At block 50,261,382 the PoolManager held about 406,197 OUSD and 19,727 pathUSD. A burn destroys part of the shared balance and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last, across every pool that uses the token. A blacklist entry or a pause freezes the full balance of that token, and policy 2 covers pathUSD and OUSD at once.
findings.preconditions: A holder of BURN_AT_ROLE, BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE or PAUSE_ROLE on the token, the token admin, or the admin of the TIP-403 policy must act. An unprivileged attacker has these roles only on tokens they created through the TIP-20 factory, which harms only pools that chose to hold that token. I could not list the current holders of BURN_AT_ROLE and BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE on OUSD and pathUSD, because the public RPC limits log queries to 100,000 blocks. I confirmed that both role constants exist on both tokens, that both tokens use policy 2, and that the PoolManager is authorized under policy 2 today.
findings.mitigations: LPs should treat every TIP-20 as an asset its issuer can burn or freeze at the PoolManager address, and check role holders and the policy admin before providing liquidity. The deployer can ask Tempo to add the PoolManager to the protected address list for burnAt and burnBlocked, and can ask issuers to confirm in writing that the PoolManager will not be blacklisted. Interfaces can warn when a pool token has a BURN_AT_ROLE holder.

findings.title: Circle's blocklist covers native USDC on Arc, so one entry for the PoolManager freezes native and ERC-20 USDC pools together
findings.difference: On Ethereum nobody can block a transfer of the native asset. On Arc the native asset is USDC, and the EVM checks Circle's blocklist on every value-bearing CALL and SELFDESTRUCT, for sender and recipient. The ERC-20 face at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 is an upgradeable proxy (admin 0x9005e53e3ee2f27999f15e7a52c58f804fc716e0, implementation 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6). That address is the only caller allowed to use the Native Coin Authority precompile, whose transfer(from, to, amount), mint and burn act on the native balance of any account, and the Native Coin Control precompile that stores the blocklist.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager holds one native balance that backs both address(0) pools and 0x3600 pools. 2. The USDC blacklister (0x2a2b7ff330f15f9a8c52af5fec27d775f5138467) blacklists the PoolManager address, and the token contract writes the entry through Native Coin Control. 3. take of address(0) runs call(gas(), to, amount, 0, 0, 0, 0) at src/types/Currency.sol:48, and the EVM reverts the value transfer because the sender is listed. take of 0x3600 calls transfer at src/types/Currency.sol:60-75, which also reverts. 4. settle with msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307, 352-354) fails because a value transfer to a listed address reverts, and ERC-20 payments to the PoolManager revert as well. 5. Every pool with either face of USDC is frozen. ERC-6909 claims still move inside the PoolManager and cannot be redeemed. collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57) reverts for both USDC currencies. 6. Separately, the proxy admin can install an implementation that calls Native Coin Authority transfer with the PoolManager as from. No PoolManager code runs in that path, so the code cannot refuse it.
findings.impact: At block 32,554,675 the PoolManager held 2,438,862 USDC as native balance. A blocklist entry freezes all of it. The EURC and cirBTC blacklisters can freeze about 20,570 EURC and 1.14 cirBTC in the same way through those tokens' own lists. An implementation upgrade could move the native balance out.
findings.preconditions: The USDC blacklister must list the PoolManager for the freeze, and the USDC proxy admin must upgrade the token for a seizure. All of these are Circle roles. An unprivileged attacker cannot reach this path. NativeCoinControl.isBlocklisted(PoolManager) and USDC.isBlacklisted(PoolManager) both return false today. I read the precompile access rules in the arc-node main branch and did not read the verified source of the token implementation at 0xc6ad664a...3ca6.
findings.mitigations: LPs on Arc should assume that Circle can freeze every USDC-denominated position in the PoolManager at once, including positions held as native value. The deployer can seek a written statement from Circle on how the PoolManager address is treated. Nothing in the PoolManager can be changed to route around a blocklist entry, so position size is the only control LPs have.

findings.title: A Stylus program used as a hook or token stops answering calls on expiry or a Stylus version change, and activation is blocked
findings.difference: On Ethereum, code at an address keeps answering calls. On Arbitrum One a contract can be a Stylus WASM program. A call to it fails unless the program was activated at the current Stylus version and its last activation or keepalive is less than 365 days old. ArbOS 61, active since 2026-08-20, moved the Stylus version from 2 to 3. On chain, ArbWasm.activationGas() is 2^64-1, which makes activateProgram fail for everyone, so a program that has expired or needs the new version cannot be brought back by its users.
findings.mechanism: Hook path: the PoolManager calls the hook with call() and reverts the whole action when the call fails. For a hook address with the before or after remove liquidity flag, modifyLiquidity with a negative delta calls the hook, so a hook that no longer answers blocks every liquidity removal in its pools. Hooks with swap or donate flags block those actions the same way. Token path: transfer and balanceOf on a Stylus token that no longer answers revert, so take, sync and settle revert for that currency in every pool. Step 1: a pool is created with a Stylus hook or a Stylus token while the program is active. Step 2: the program reaches 365 days without a keepalive, or an ArbOS upgrade changes the Stylus version. getActiveProgram returns ProgramExpired or ProgramNeedsUpgrade and the call fails. Step 3: anyone who tries activateProgram is charged activationGas first, which exceeds any gas limit, so the call fails. Keepalive works only while the program is still active and at least 31 days old. ArbOS 61 also removed WASM multi-value support, so a program that relies on it cannot be reactivated even when activation reopens. I did not enumerate which pools on Arbitrum One use a Stylus hook or token, and I did not establish the date on which activation gas was raised, so I cannot say how many programs missed the move to version 3.
findings.impact: LP principal and fees in pools whose hook gates liquidity removal are stuck for as long as activation stays closed. For a Stylus token, every balance of that token in the PoolManager is stuck. No funds move to an attacker. Pools without Stylus hooks or tokens are unaffected.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use a Stylus program as its hook or as one of its currencies. Then either nobody pays for keepalive within the 365 day window, or governance ships a Stylus version change. No attacker action is required and none can speed it up. The Arbitrum Foundation or Security Council can reopen activation.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators on Arbitrum One should prefer EVM hooks. LPs in a pool with a Stylus hook should check ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft for the hook and for each token, and anyone can pay codehashKeepalive once the program is 31 days old. A hook author can leave the remove liquidity flags unset so that removals never depend on the hook.

findings.title: A pool's hook can block or reprice every liquidity removal in that pool, and core has no path that skips the hook
findings.difference: None. The code path is the same on every network. Networks where the code behind an address can change after pool creation (A7) add ways for a hook that was harmless at creation to start doing this.
findings.mechanism: modifyLiquidity calls the hook library's beforeModifyLiquidity before it touches the pool (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity when address bit 9 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts the whole call when the hook reverts (Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or carries the wrong selector (Hooks.sol:152-154). A hook address with no code returns empty data, so it also reverts. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set, and when bit 0 is also set it reads a BalanceDelta from the return data, subtracts it from the caller's delta without any bound and credits it to the hook (Hooks.sol:232-243, src/PoolManager.sol:177-183). The hook call is skipped only when msg.sender is the hook itself (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). No other function removes liquidity. The swap path has the same shape: beforeSwap and afterSwap deltas move value between swapper and hook (Hooks.sol:248-315), and the hook of a dynamic fee pool can set the LP fee to 100 percent (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
findings.impact: Principal and uncollected fees of every position in the affected pool. A reverting hook freezes them. A hook with the return delta bit can take part or all of what a removal would pay out, up to what the LP's router accepts. Funds in other pools are not reachable this way, because the caller delta plus the hook delta always equals the pool delta (Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312) and each party must net to zero before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112).
findings.preconditions: The pool's hook address has bit 9 (0x200) or bit 8 (0x100) set, and for taking funds also bit 0. The hook code reverts, returns a bad selector, returns a hostile delta, or is replaced or removed after LPs deposit. LPs must have chosen that pool. This is how the hook design works; I list it because it is a path to a freeze or loss that the text of core does not limit.
findings.mitigations: LPs and position managers can read the low 14 bits of the hook address before depositing and treat bits 9, 8 and 0 as custody risk unless the hook code is immutable and reviewed. Routers should enforce minimum amounts on removal so a hostile return delta reverts. The deployer cannot change this without adding a removal path that skips hooks.

verification.factCheck: The finding claims no network difference, so the chain facts to check are its remark that code behind a hook address can change after pool creation and whether the repository expects the behaviour. I fetched EIP-7702, status Final. It says each authorization writes the delegation indicator 0xef0100 || address into the authorizing account's code, that a later authorization can point elsewhere or clear the code, and that code executing operations load the code the delegation points to. An externally owned account whose low 14 bits carry hook flags can therefore act as a hook, and its owner can replace or remove the logic later. I fetched EIP-6780, which limits account deletion by SELFDESTRUCT to the transaction that created the contract. On chain, eth_getCode on Arbitrum One for 0xa853180523bd16fa6a9c449ab050e108da642488 returned 0xef01001947e2c7b5ca44f2db6236cf5ac3e23457e8a488, which is a delegation indicator at an address whose low bits set beforeInitialize, afterAddLiquidity, beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnsDelta. I did not confirm that an initialized pool uses that address, and it does not carry the removal bits 9 or 8. The repository's own tests expect the behaviour the finding describes. test/PoolManager.t.sol:272-287 expects a removal to revert with InvalidHookResponse when the hook returns a wrong selector. test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:297-322 expects a hook to receive 5.43 percent of a withdrawal through the afterRemoveLiquidity return delta.
verification.codeCheck: modifyLiquidity is the only function that changes a position (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184). It calls beforeModifyLiquidity before the pool update (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 with bit 9 set the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts when the call fails (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or the selector differs (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). A call to an address without code succeeds with empty return data and then fails the length check. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:233-241), requires exactly 64 bytes of return data when bit 0 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:166) and subtracts the returned delta from the caller's delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:242). The subtraction is bounded only by the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). The hook delta is credited to the hook address and the remainder to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183). The only bypass is a call where msg.sender is the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). I looked for a guard the finding missed and found none: there is no removal path without the hook call and no cap on the return delta. The caller delta and the hook delta always sum to the pool delta, and unlock reverts unless every delta is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112), so funds of other pools are out of reach, and a return delta larger than the payout succeeds only when the LP's own unlock callback pays the shortfall. The swap path matches the description (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:248-315), and updateDynamicLPFee accepts any fee up to 1,000,000 from the hook of a dynamic fee pool (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
verification.corrections: The difference field presents changing code as a property of some networks. EIP-7702 delegation and upgradeable proxy hooks make it possible on every network that has activated EIP-7702, Ethereum included, so the exposure does not depend on the network. The freeze case needs nothing from the LP. The taking case needs the LP's router to accept the reduced amount, as the finding says. The add liquidity path has the same shape through bits 11, 10 and 1, which can block or surcharge deposits and cannot hold existing funds. Severity stays medium because the loss is limited to pools whose LPs chose that hook address, and the tests show this is the intended trust model.

findings.title: Uncollected fees above the int128 maximum make every later update of a liquidity position revert
findings.difference: None. The condition is the same on every network. It needs a token whose supply in base units is larger than 2^127 - 1, about 1.7e38. The comment at src/libraries/Pool.sol:403 says the code assumes token supply stays within uint128.
findings.mechanism: Every modifyLiquidity call, including a zero delta poke and a removal, runs Position.update and then casts both fee amounts with feesOwed0.toInt128() and feesOwed1.toInt128() (src/libraries/Pool.sol:184-192). Position.update computes the fee as (feeGrowthInside - feeGrowthInsideLast) * liquidity / 2^128 for the whole position (src/libraries/Position.sol:92-97). SafeCast.toInt128(uint256) reverts for values of 2^127 or more (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). Because the whole call reverts, the position's fee checkpoint is never updated. The amount owed therefore never goes down, and every later call for that position reverts the same way, whatever liquidityDelta is used. Fees reach a position through swaps (Pool.sol:401-407) and through donate (Pool.sol:466-480). Each single donate or swap is capped at int128, so the threshold is crossed over two or more calls. I confirmed the arithmetic with a Python transcription of Pool, Position and SafeCast: after two donations of 2^126 + 10 units to a range with one position, updates with delta 0, -1, -1e18 and +1 all revert.
findings.impact: The principal in both currencies and the uncollected fees of that one position stay in the PoolManager with no way out. Other positions in the pool and other pools are not affected.
findings.preconditions: One position must be owed 2^127 base units or more of one currency in fees that it has not yet collected. Fees owed are real tokens paid by swappers or donors, so the token's supply in base units must exceed 1.7e38 and a payer must give up that amount. For a token with a supply below that bound the state cannot be reached. A party that controls such a token's supply can already drain the other side of the pool by selling, so this adds a way to freeze but no extra profit.
findings.mitigations: LPs can avoid pools with a token whose base unit supply exceeds 2^127, and can collect fees with a zero delta call before the amount owed gets near the bound. Pool creators can check totalSupply and decimals. A code change that caps or splits the fee credit would remove the condition.

verification.factCheck: The finding states no network difference and I found none, because the path uses no chain feature. No external source applies, so the facts are in the repository. I recomputed the arithmetic on my own. Two donations of 2^126 + 10 base units into a range with one position give a fee growth for which Position.update returns 2^127 + 19 or 2^127 + 20 for position liquidity of 1, 1e6, 1e18 and about 2^100. Each value is at or above the bound where SafeCast.toInt128 reverts. No test covers the case. test/PoolManager.t.sol:908-915 bounds a single donation to the int128 maximum, and test/libraries/Position.t.sol:26-70 fuzzes Position.update without the cast that follows it in Pool. Two links are unconfirmed. I could not confirm whether any token held by a deployed PoolManager has a base unit supply above 2^127 - 1, which is the researcher's open lead. I did not exercise the path on the deployed contracts, because it needs an unlock callback and a read only call cannot reach it.
verification.codeCheck: Pool.modifyLiquidity calls Position.update for every liquidityDelta, including zero and negative values, and then casts both fee amounts with toInt128 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:183-193). Position.update computes fees on the full liquidity held before the update (src/libraries/Position.sol:82, 92-97). SafeCast.toInt128(uint256) reverts at 2^127 (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). The revert undoes the checkpoint write at src/libraries/Position.sol:100-101, so the amount owed can stay or grow and cannot shrink. The ticks of a position that holds liquidity keep a nonzero liquidityGross, so their feeGrowthOutside values are set once and are cleared only when the last position leaves (src/libraries/Pool.sol:533-539, 196-203). Fee growth inside the range can therefore not be lowered by anyone. Wrapping the growth difference past 2^256 would take further real payments of roughly 2^128 times the position liquidity less the amount already owed, which for any realistic liquidity is far more than a uint128 supply. Pool.donate caps one donation below 2^127 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:471) and the casts on the swap delta cap one swap (src/libraries/Pool.sol:454-460), so the bound is crossed over two or more payments. The owed fees are backed by tokens: a donor who shares the range receives only its own pro rata share back, so the victim's share has to be paid in. There is no partial fee collection and no other exit, so the principal of that position in both currencies stays in the PoolManager.
verification.corrections: Severity raised from low to medium. The scale reserves low for hazards with no direct loss path, and this is a direct and permanent freeze of a position, limited to pools with a token whose base unit supply exceeds 2^127 - 1. The actor is any holder of 2^127 base units who gives them up as a donation or as swap fees, or ordinary swap volume against a passive position that never collects. The bound is 2^127, half of the uint128 supply that the comment at src/libraries/Pool.sol:403 names as the assumption, so a token inside the stated assumption with a supply between 2^127 and 2^128 can still reach it. The finding's point that an issuer with unlimited supply can already empty the pool by selling holds, and it does not cover a third party token with a large fixed supply, where the attacker gains nothing and the LP still loses access to both currencies of the position.
